title: Genotype and Environment (Water Temperature) Interactions on the Growth and Feed Efficiency of the Spotted Babylon Babylonia areolata
content:
ABSTRACT

Babylonia areolata is an emerging aquaculture species in China. Feed costs represent 40%–60% of its total production expenses, making feed efficiency a key target for genetic improvement. Water temperature is a major environmental factor in the cultivation of B. areolata, as it varies considerably across seasons, geographic regions and culture systems. Therefore, a thorough understanding of feed efficiency traits under different temperature conditions, as well as genotype-by-environment interactions, is essential for evaluating breeding success and developing effective breeding strategies. This study shows that growth traits in B. areolata have moderate to high heritability under three water temperature conditions. The feed efficiency ratio (FER) varied substantially across temperatures, whereas residual feed intake (RFI) consistently exhibited low to moderate heritability. Strong genetic correlations were observed between FER and specific growth rate (SGR) under all temperature regimes, whereas genetic and phenotypic correlations among other traits varied significantly with temperature. Analysis of genotype-by-environment interactions revealed that genetic correlation coefficients for growth traits exceeded 0.9 between environments, indicating negligible interaction effects. In contrast, FER showed moderate interaction, with coefficients ranging from 0.593 to 0.776, whereas RFI exhibited values close to zero, suggesting strong interaction effects. This study suggests that FER may be a more practical trait for selection in feed efficiency breeding, given its favourable genetic correlation with growth and its comparatively lower G × E interaction, whereas RFI appears to be more sensitive to temperature changes. This study provides important theoretical support for the selective breeding of feed efficiency traits in the B. areolata.
